one_liner: Boost's C++ object-graph serializer; its native binary archive round-tripped a ~17 KB record ~1.9x faster than Protobuf.
what_it_does: Boost's general-purpose C++ serialization library. You write one serialize(Archive&, unsigned version) member or free function per type (free functions let you serialize classes you cannot change), then stream objects into text, XML or native binary archives with ar << obj and ar >> obj. It covers STL containers, deep pointer save/restore with tracking of shared objects, polymorphic pointers through registration/export, and per-class versioning so newer code can read older files. It does not replace Protobuf directly: there is no IDL, schema or code generator, and archives can only be read by C++ programs.
how_it_is_fast: Nothing in the library targets speed. It won this benchmark because the native binary archive does almost no encoding. basic_binary_oprimitive::save writes each primitive as sizeof(T) raw native bytes with a single streambuf sputn, with no varint or zigzag step. std::vector of arithmetic types takes the 'array optimization' path: use_array_optimization is keyed on is_bitwise_serializable, which defaults to is_arithmetic, so the whole buffer goes out in one save_binary call. The benchmark's Protobuf schema declares the ids as proto3 repeated int64, which Protobuf varint-encodes (negative values take all 10 bytes), so on this int-heavy record a fixed-width bulk copy beats encoding and decoding each value.
when_to_use: C++-only persistence or checkpointing of existing class hierarchies that hold raw pointers, shared_ptr graphs or polymorphic base pointers, where mapping everything onto .proto messages would be a rewrite.
Records dominated by std::vector of arithmetic types (int64, double) written to binary_oarchive: the bulk save_binary path writes them as a single raw copy.
Many objects, or a few large ones, per archive (files, snapshots, bulk IPC), so the per-archive setup cost is amortized.
Codebases already built against Boost that need non-intrusive serialization of third-party types, or per-class versioning so old files still load.
Writer and reader on the same platform and ABI, which the native binary archive assumes.
when_not_to_use: Cross-language interchange, or wire contracts shared with other teams: there is no schema or IDL and no non-C++ reader. Stay on Protobuf, or see Thrift/hpp-proto.

Deserializing untrusted input such as network data from clients. Issue #331 (insecure deserialization leading to type and ownership confusion, reported against 1.89.0 and below) is still open with details withheld, and a negative-class-id check was only added in August 2026 (#332).

Small messages with one archive each. The maintainer measured 14.2 us per ~70-byte message with a fresh stream and archive per message versus 0.21 us with one shared archive (MSVC x64, issue #347), so setup dominates.

When wire size or top C++ speed matters. It had the largest payload in the benchmark's main table (17,470 B vs Protobuf 16,116 and msgpack 13,402), and in the same run cereal (1052 ms) and yas (302.7 ms) were faster.

Binary archives that must move across architectures. The native binary archive refuses to load when int/long/float/double sizes or endianness differ, and the portable binary archive lives only in the examples directory, without portable floating point.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (compiled boost_serialization, plus boost_wserialization for wide-char archives), usually taken from a Boost distribution
integration.dependencies: Boost: array, assert, config, core, detail, integer, io, iterator, move, mpl, optional, predef, preprocessor, smart_ptr, spirit, type_traits, unordered, utility, variant (public); function (private)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (meta/libraries.json cxxstd 11); CI covers GCC 7-16, Clang 6-22, MSVC 14.3/14.5 and Apple Clang
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (MSVC, clang-win, MinGW GCC) in CI; the code is architecture-neutral, but native binary archives only load on a matching platform (sizes and endianness are checked in the header)
integration.thread_safety: Documented: never share one archive instance between threads; separate archives in separate threads are fine, because the shared type tables are lock-free singletons initialized at module load. Do not load or unload DLLs/shared objects while any archive is open.

gotchas: Objects are tracked by memory address. Saving successive copies from the same stack variable silently writes only the first one (a const-reference static assert catches the common case, but not inside name-value pairs), and after loading into a temporary and moving it into a container you must call reset_object_address or pointer restoration breaks.

Polymorphic pointers must be registered or exported. BOOST_CLASS_EXPORT has to come after the archive headers are included, and each type needs exactly one BOOST_CLASS_EXPORT_IMPLEMENT. Getting this wrong fails at run time with unregistered_class, or with duplicate symbols at link time.

Binary archives need streams opened with std::ios::binary. Otherwise CRLF translation corrupts the archive, and the library cannot detect it until load (debug builds assert). By default each archive also writes a header and swaps in a codecvt facet; the no_header and no_codecvt flags turn these off.
Lengths read from the archive are trusted. The binary load of std::string reads a size_t and calls s.resize(l) with no bound, so a malformed or hostile archive can force a huge allocation.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: cereal ran the same benchmark slightly faster (1052 vs 1195 ms) and is header-only with no dependencies, but its docs say it does not serialize raw pointers or references. Pick Boost.Serialization when you need raw-pointer object graphs with address tracking or must read existing Boost archives; otherwise take cereal. Choose Apache Thrift binary (1190 ms, a tie here) or hpp-proto if you need an IDL or cross-language wire format.
verified_claims_summary: Source: the third-party thekvs/cpp-serializers shootout, 2019 README table (boost 1.69.0 vs protobuf 3.7.0 and msgpack 3.1.1; Intel Core i7, Ubuntu 16.04; CMake Release build, clang 5.0.0 per the commit that published the table; standard library not stated). One record of 1,000 int64 plus 100 copies of an 86-char string (~17 KB) was round-tripped through a fresh binary_oarchive/binary_iarchive over stringstreams each iteration. Boost took 1195.04 ms total against 2312.78 ms for Protobuf (~1.9x) and 2560.6 ms for msgpack (~2.1x); nothing was compared against a std facility, and the '1,000,000 operations' label looks too large for these totals, though the ratios are unaffected.
status_note: Actively maintained (commits through 2026-09-25; Gennaro Prota took over maintenance in 2026 and has been closing old issues) and shipped in every Boost release under BSL-1.0. Easy to get from system Boost packages or the Boost CMake superproject, but it is a compiled library with about 20 Boost dependencies, not a single header you can vendor.
